reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Presents as a distinctive drug-resistant epilepsy, characteristically with prolonged episodes of nonconvulsive status epilepticus marked by subtle confusion and behavioural change
Seizures usually begin in childhood in a previously well-developing child, with cognitive and behavioural decline following seizure onset
A characteristic EEG shows prolonged runs of high-voltage slow waves with intermixed spikes, often during nonconvulsive status
The ring frequently forms with little or no loss of material, so the karyotype can look almost balanced and copy-number tests may be normal
Low-level mosaicism is common, and a higher proportion of ring-bearing cells tends to accompany earlier onset and more severe disease
Malformations and dysmorphism are usually mild or absent, in contrast to most other ring syndromes
Behavioural disturbance and nocturnal frontal-type seizures are frequently reported
reference.pathophysiology: Ring chromosome 20 usually forms by fusion of the chromosome ends with little or no loss of genetic material, so many cases are effectively complete rings. The epilepsy phenotype is thought to arise from disturbance of genes near the telomeric regions, including those implicated in other epilepsies, together with the instability and abnormal behaviour of the ring during cell division, rather than from simple gene deletion. Mosaicism for the ring is typical, and a larger proportion of ring-containing cells is generally associated with earlier and more severe disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Frontal lobe epilepsy of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype analysing a sufficient number of cells to detect low-level mosaicism
EEG, including prolonged or ambulatory recording to capture nonconvulsive status
Chromosomal microarray, recognising it is frequently normal because material is not lost
MRI of the brain, which is usually unremarkable
Neuropsychological assessment to track cognition and behaviour
redFlags: Prolonged nonconvulsive status epilepticus with altered awareness
Cognitive or behavioural regression after seizure onset
reference.prognosis: Seizures are typically refractory to medication and often lifelong, and cognitive and behavioural decline tends to progress with ongoing seizures, although intellect may be relatively preserved early in the course.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal microarray excludes a chromosomal cause, since the ring often involves no copy-number loss
Analysing too few cells and thereby missing low-level mosaicism
Mistaking nonconvulsive status for a primary behavioural or psychiatric disturbance
Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with unexplained refractory epilepsy and normal imaging
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gardner and Sutherland's Chromosome Abnormalities and Genetic Counseling
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medications (such as valproate, lamotrigine or levetiracetam) as the mainstay, while anticipating drug-resistant seizures
Prompt recognition and treatment of recurrent nonconvulsive status epilepticus, including benzodiazepine rescue protocols for prolonged episodes
Non-pharmacological options for refractory epilepsy such as the ketogenic diet or vagus nerve stimulation, as resective surgery is generally unhelpful given the diffuse genetic basis
Serial neuropsychological assessment with educational and behavioural support to address the cognitive and behavioural decline that follows seizure onset
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology and epilepsy specialist involvement for ongoing seizure and developmental management
Genetic counselling with karyotype confirmation, discussing the usually de novo occurrence and the role of mosaicism
